text: In 2001, one rapper played a single diss track at a concert in New York, and started a war that produced maybe the greatest diss song ever recorded. In 2024, another diss track ended up as the Record of the Year at the Grammys, and on the biggest stage in American television. And in between? Careers destroyed, labels collapsed, two of the greatest rappers of all time dead before thirty. Today, we go through all of it.

title: EVERY MAJOR RAP BEEF EXPLAINED
text: I'm ze Brofessor of Beats, and today I explain every major beef in hip-hop history. Twelve wars, fifty years. How each one started, how it ended, and who actually won. No cap, just facts. And here's the thing to keep in mind the whole way through: beef is not a bug in hip-hop. It is a feature. Rap was born as a competition, and every one of these wars changed the rules of that competition. So grab a notebook. Class is in session.

title: BUSY BEE vs KOOL MOE DEE
text: Every beef on this list exists because of one night in December 1981. Busy Bee Starski was the king of party rap. Call and response, crowd-pleasing routines, simple rhymes, everybody having a good time. At a Christmas battle at the Harlem World club, he did his usual routine, and the crowd loved it. Then Kool Moe Dee of the Treacherous Three grabbed the mic. And instead of rocking the crowd, he attacked Busy Bee directly. By name. Line after line, he dismantled his style, called it childish, called it recycled, called it a joke. Nobody had ever done that before. Up to that point, MCs were hosts. Their job was to keep the party going. The recording of that night spread on cassette tapes across New York like a virus. People who were never in that club could recite the lines. In one night, rap stopped being just a party trick and became a competitive sport, where skill could be measured, and where you could lose in public. Every diss track you have ever heard traces back to that stage. But the first beef that actually sold records? That was started by a fourteen-year-old girl.

title: THE ROXANNE WARS
text: In 1984, the group UTFO released Roxanne, Roxanne. A song complaining about a fictional girl who rejected all of them. It was a hit. A fourteen-year-old from the Queensbridge projects named Lolita Shante Gooden heard it, and with producer Marley Marl she recorded an answer, reportedly in a single take. Roxanne's Revenge. She rapped as Roxanne, and she destroyed every member of the group. The record sold in the hundreds of thousands. UTFO responded by bringing out their own, official, Real Roxanne. And then things got completely out of control. Over the next year, somewhere between thirty and a hundred different Roxanne answer records were released. Roxanne's sister. Roxanne's parents. Roxanne's doctor. A whole cottage industry built on one fictional woman. It sounds ridiculous, and it was. But the Roxanne Wars proved something the record industry never forgot: beef sells. It also made Roxanne Shante the first battle queen of hip-hop, as a teenager. The next war, though, wasn't about a girl. It was about geography.

title: THE BRIDGE WARS
text: 1986. MC Shan and producer Marley Marl of the Juice Crew release The Bridge. A tribute to their home, the Queensbridge projects in Queens. Across the river, a young KRS-One of Boogie Down Productions hears it as a claim that hip-hop started in Queensbridge. Which, to anyone from the Bronx, is blasphemy. Hip-hop was born in the Bronx, in 1973, at a back to school party on Sedgwick Avenue. Shan always said he never meant it that way. KRS did not care. His responses, South Bronx, and then The Bridge Is Over, were so devastating that they essentially defined how you win a beef. Not by being angrier. By being catchier. The Bridge Is Over is a dancehall-flavored track that is still played in clubs today, almost forty years later. Shan's career never fully recovered, and KRS-One became the self-appointed teacher of hip-hop. Lesson number one of rap warfare: the winner is whoever makes the diss you can dance to. For the next few years, beef was still mostly about pride and neighborhoods. Then it got personal. Between former brothers.

title: ICE CUBE vs N.W.A
text: N.W.A were the most dangerous group in America. Straight Outta Compton made the FBI send a letter to their label. And Ice Cube wrote a huge part of it. In 1989, Cube left the group in a dispute over money. He believed manager Jerry Heller was underpaying him, and he refused to sign a contract he thought was unfair. The rest of the group mocked him on their next records, calling him a traitor. Cube waited. Then, on his 1991 album Death Certificate, he released No Vaseline. Four and a half minutes aimed at every member of N.W.A, and at Jerry Heller, with lines so brutal that people still rank it among the coldest diss tracks ever recorded. N.W.A never released a real answer. The group fell apart soon after, with Dr. Dre leaving to start Death Row Records. The happy ending came years later: Cube and Dre reunited, made music together, and in 2015 the movie Straight Outta Compton told the whole story. But No Vaseline proved something important. A diss could break up a group, and outlive it. And the label that was born from that breakup, Death Row, would be at the center of the darkest beef of all.

title: TUPAC vs THE NOTORIOUS B.I.G.
text: This is the biggest beef in hip-hop history, and the one with no winners. Tupac Shakur and Biggie Smalls started as friends. Pac took Biggie on the road, gave him advice, they performed together. In November 1994, Tupac was shot five times in the lobby of Quad Studios in New York, and robbed. He survived. And he became convinced that Biggie and Bad Boy Records, run by Sean Puffy Combs, knew about it in advance. Biggie denied it for the rest of his life. A few months later, Biggie released Who Shot Ya. He said it was recorded before the shooting. Pac heard it as a confession. From there, a personal conflict became a coastal war. Pac signed with Suge Knight's Death Row Records in Los Angeles, Bad Boy ran New York, and the media poured gasoline on everything. West versus East. Pac's Hit Em Up remains the most vicious diss ever recorded. Pure, open hatred, with nothing held back. In September 1996, Tupac was shot in Las Vegas and died six days later. He was twenty-five. Six months after that, in March 1997, Biggie was shot and killed in Los Angeles. He was twenty-four. For almost three decades, both cases looked unsolvable. Then in 2023, Las Vegas police arrested Duane Keffe D Davis and charged him in connection with Tupac's murder. I will do a full lecture on this one, the timeline, the theories, the investigations, because it deserves much more than two minutes. Here, the point is this. After 1997, hip-hop learned exactly where the line is. And the next great war deliberately stayed on wax.

title: JAY-Z vs NAS
sub: The war for the New York throne
text: New York, 2001. The throne Biggie left empty had two serious claimants: Jay-Z and Nas. For years they traded subliminal shots, lines that never used a name but everyone understood. Then, at Hot 97's Summer Jam in 2001, Jay premiered Takeover. A cold, factual demolition of Nas's career. One classic album, then nothing. A one-hot-album-every-ten-year average. At the time, a lot of people agreed. Nas was considered washed. Then he answered with Ether. Pure, concentrated disrespect. Sound effects of gunshots, the name Jay-Z bleeped into Gay-Z, line after line about stealing Biggie's style. It was so effective that ether became a verb. To ether someone means to destroy them so completely that they cannot come back. Jay responded with Super Ugly, and went so far below the belt, with details about Nas's personal life, that his own mother reportedly told him to apologize, and he did, on the radio. Who won? Hot 97 ran a listener poll, and Nas won it. History says: both. The beef revived Nas's career, it gave Jay his hunger back, and both men released some of their best albums during the war. In 2005, Jay brought Nas on stage at his I Declare War concert, and they ended it in front of everyone. A year later, Nas signed to Def Jam, where Jay was president. The perfect beef. Two legends, zero funerals, and three classic records. Now, quick reminder before we continue. If you already learned something today, hit subscribe, it costs nothing and it keeps this class running. Because the next one wasn't a war of poets. It was a hostile corporate takeover, disguised as a beef.

title: 50 CENT vs JA RULE
text: Early 2000s. Ja Rule is one of the biggest stars on the planet. Melodic hooks, duets with Jennifer Lopez and Ashanti, number ones on the pop charts. His label, Murder Inc., run by Irv Gotti, is printing money. 50 Cent was a Queens mixtape rapper with a genuine street conflict with Ja's circle, going back to a robbery and a stabbing at a studio. In 2000, 50 was shot nine times and survived. Two years later he signed with Eminem and Dr. Dre, and he weaponized all of that history. Not one diss, but a total campaign. Wanksta, Back Down, skits, interviews, constant, relentless mockery of Ja Rule singing on pop records while pretending to be a gangster. And it worked like nothing before or since. Get Rich or Die Tryin' became one of the best-selling debut albums of all time. Ja Rule's sales collapsed. And on top of that, federal investigators went after Murder Inc. over alleged ties to a drug kingpin. Gotti was eventually acquitted, but the label never recovered its power. Within about three years, the biggest act in rap had become a punchline. 50 proved that a beef can be a marketing strategy. A planned demolition of a competitor, designed to take his market share. Cold-blooded. And it built an empire. Speaking of 50's boss, you cannot make a beef list without the man nobody ever beat.

title: EMINEM vs EVERYBODY
text: Eminem doesn't have a beef. Eminem has a career-long policy. In the early 2000s, The Source magazine and its co-owner Benzino called him a culture thief and tried to destroy his credibility. They even dug up an old tape of a teenage Eminem saying racist things. Em apologized for the tape, and then responded with Nail in the Coffin and The Sauce. The Source had been the bible of hip-hop. Its credibility never recovered. When Ja Rule went at him during the 50 Cent war, the answer was a song with a brutal rhyme scheme and a simple message: do not mention my daughter. But the modern classic is Machine Gun Kelly. Back in 2012, MGK tweeted that Eminem's daughter Hailie was hot. She was sixteen. Em held on to that for six years. In 2018, on his album Kamikaze, he took a shot. MGK answered with Rap Devil, which, honestly, is a genuinely good diss track. Eminem answered in days with Killshot, which became the biggest twenty-four-hour debut for a hip-hop song on YouTube at the time. And then MGK switched genres entirely, and became a pop punk artist. When your opponent leaves the entire sport, that is a technical knockout. Undefeated. But no diss on this list ended a career faster than number nine.

title: DRAKE vs MEEK MILL
text: Summer 2015. Meek Mill is engaged to Nicki Minaj, he has a number one album, and he is on tour with her. Then he tweets that Drake does not write his own raps, and that he has a ghostwriter. In hip-hop, that is still a capital offense. Meek even pointed at a specific writer, Quentin Miller. The internet waits for a war. Drake drops Charged Up, a slow, almost lazy warning. People say it's weak. Then, before Meek even answers, Back to Back. Fast, funny, and built for the internet. Is that a world tour or your girl's tour. Within hours it was everywhere, on every timeline, as a meme. Drake performed it at his own festival in front of a screen showing memes of Meek. Meek's response, Wanna Know, came days too late, and landed flat. That was it. Two songs, about a week, and career damage that took Meek years to repair. Back to Back even became the first diss track ever nominated for a Grammy. The lesson: in the social media era, a beef isn't won with bars alone. It is won with memes and speed. But Drake's story doesn't end there. Because the ghostwriting question never went away.

title: PUSHA T vs DRAKE
text: Drake and Pusha T had been trading subliminal shots for more than a decade, going back to Pusha's group Clipse and to Drake's mentor, Lil Wayne. In 2018 it finally detonated. On his album Daytona, Pusha raps on Infrared about Drake's ghostwriters. Drake responds within hours with Duppy Freestyle. Confident, mocking, and he even sends Pusha an invoice for promotional services. Funny. Then Pusha T drops The Story of Adidon, and changes the rules of engagement forever. He reveals to the world that Drake has a secret son. He uses a real old photo of Drake in blackface makeup as the cover art. Drake later explained the photo was from an acting job about racial stereotypes. It did not matter. No jokes, no punchlines. A surgical strike, built on opposition research. Drake never responded. J Prince, his mentor, said publicly that he stopped Drake from releasing the response he had recorded, because it was too damaging. A few weeks later, Drake confirmed the son on his own album. Pusha won on points nobody knew were on the scoreboard, and taught every rapper alive that receipts beat rhymes. Before we get to the main event, one war that proved the women of rap play by the same rules.

title: NICKI MINAJ vs REMY MA
text: For years, Nicki Minaj was the undisputed queen of rap, and she was not shy about it. Remy Ma, a Bronx rapper and protegee of Big Pun and Fat Joe, had spent six years in prison and came home to a scene where Nicki ruled everything. The tension went back to the late 2000s, with subliminal lines in both directions. In early 2017, Nicki took shots on a remix and on a Gucci Mane track. Remy's answer came out in February 2017, and the title told you everything. shETHER. Over the instrumental of Nas's Ether. Almost seven minutes, attacking Nicki's career, her credibility, her relationships, her family. It was so brutal that people asked whether it was even allowed. Nicki answered with No Frauds, featuring Drake and Lil Wayne, which charted, but most fans gave the round to Remy. The beef did not end Nicki's career. She is still one of the biggest artists in the world. But shETHER proved that the oldest beat in the war book still works, and that a diss written with fire and a long memory can beat a superstar's machine. And that brings us to the main event. The biggest beef of the modern era.

title: KENDRICK LAMAR vs DRAKE
text: Kendrick Lamar and Drake circled each other for over a decade. In 2013, on Big Sean's Control, Kendrick named Drake, J. Cole, and others, and said he was trying to murder all of them, musically. Then came ten years of subliminals. In March 2024, on Like That, with Future and Metro Boomin, Kendrick ends the big three conversation. Forget the big three, he says. It is just big me. What followed was the fastest, highest-stakes exchange in beef history. Drake fires Push Ups. Then Taylor Made Freestyle, using AI-generated voices of Tupac and Snoop Dogg, which he had to take down after Tupac's estate threatened to sue. Kendrick answers with Euphoria, six minutes of pure contempt. Then 6:16 in LA. Drake responds with Family Matters. And then, within about an hour, Kendrick releases Meet the Grahams. And the next day, Not Like Us. Accusations from both sides got genuinely dark, and most of them were never proven. But Not Like Us became something no diss track had ever been. A global number one hit. A song played at weddings and in stadiums. In February 2025 it won Record of the Year and Song of the Year at the Grammys. A week later, Kendrick performed it at the Super Bowl halftime show, in front of the biggest audience in halftime history. Drake later sued his own label, Universal Music Group, claiming the song defamed him. In October 2025, a federal judge dismissed the case. Fifty years after Kool Moe Dee grabbed that mic in Harlem, a battle rap performance headlined the biggest stage in American entertainment. The sport Busy Bee lost that night became the sport everybody watches.

title: HONORABLE MENTIONS
sub: Wars that almost made the list
text: Before the final lesson, a few honorable mentions, because twelve is not enough for fifty years of war. LL Cool J versus Kool Moe Dee, the original veteran against the new superstar, which ran for years in the late eighties. Common versus Ice Cube, where a Chicago backpack rapper went at a West Coast legend with Bitch in Yoo, and lived to tell the tale. Lil Kim versus Foxy Brown, the queens of nineties New York, a rivalry that ended with a shootout outside a radio station and a perjury conviction. The Game versus 50 Cent and G-Unit, a war between former labelmates that went on for years. And Cardi B versus Nicki Minaj, which turned physical at a New York Fashion Week party in 2018. Every one of these could be its own lecture. Tell me which one you want first.

title: WHAT DID WE LEARN?
text: So, what did we learn? Beef is hip-hop's engine. It made careers, it ended careers, it broke up groups, it collapsed labels, and twice, it ended lives. And if you look at all twelve wars, the winners were never simply the angriest. They were the catchiest, like KRS-One. The most strategic, like 50 Cent. The fastest, like Drake in 2015. The ones with receipts, like Pusha T. And the ones who turned a diss into a song the whole world wanted to sing, like Kendrick. Now tell me in the comments: which beef did I forget, and who do you think really won Jay-Z versus Nas? If you learned something today, subscribe. New class every Tuesday and Friday. Next lecture: every gang sign and symbol in rap videos, explained. You have seen them a thousand times. You have no idea what they mean. Class dismissed. See you there.
